Guiding Green Choices: The Impact of Pre-Checkout
GHG-Reducing Product Swap Recommendations
Kevin O’Sullivana,d, Verena Tiefenbeckb, Sybilla Merianc, Sabrina Stöcklic, Elgar Fleischa,
Martin Natterc
aChair of Information Management, ETH Zurich, Weinbergstrasse 56, 8092 Zurich, Switzerland
bSchool of Business, Economics and Society, Lange Gasse 20, 90403 Nuremberg, Germany
cChair of Marketing, University of Zurich, Plattenstrasse 14, 8032 Zurich, Switzerland
dCorresponding author: kosullivan@ethz.ch
Shifting diets from animal products towards more plant-based foods is generally accepted
as an essential measure to reduce the environmental impacts of the global food system
[1, 2, 3]. A shift from current diets to diets that exclude animal-based products would re-
duce the food system’s land use by 76% [4] and greenhouse gas emissions (GHG) by around
50% [4]. While dietary change of any magnitude is difficult to achieve [5, 6, 7], sweeping
dietary changes, such as eliminating or drastically reducing animal product consumption,
are particularly difficult to achieve and maintain. A promising, alternative strategy to large
scale dietary is targeting the small, simple changes that lead to meaningful reductions in
environmental impacts. Research on US populations suggests that dietary carbon footprint
could be reduced by 33% - 35% through small, targeted substitutions [3, 8], such as substi-
tuting 10% of beef intake with plant-based foods [3] or by swapping high-carbon meats for
low-carbon meats [8].
In light of the promising potential of targeted, small changes, we conducted a randomised
controlled trial (RCT) in a hypothetical online supermarket environment to investigate con-
sumers’ responses to GHG-reducing product swap recommendations, as well as their resulting
GHG reductions. The study was preregistered and incentive-compatible. Participants were
presented with a shopping basket typical of the average 2-person German household and
were instructed to proceed through the online supermarket. Prior to checkout, participants
landed on the treatment page where there was an explanation on how swapping animal prod-
ucts for plant-based alternatives can meaningully lower GHG, and in addition, all animal
products in their shopping basket were displayed alongside an option to swap to the closest
plant-based alternative (e.g. plant-based chicken instead of chicken). Participants were ran-
domized to one of the four experimental groups: a targeted treatment group, T(Targeted),
where the most effective GHG-reducing product swap was explicitly highlighted; an infor-
mation treatment group, T(Info), where the percentage GHG reduction resulting from each
swap was presented; a targeted and information group, T(Targeted x Info), a combination
of T(Targeted) and T(Info); and lastly, the control group, C, where the products swaps
were displayed without GHG reduction information and without any indication of the most
effective GHG-reducing product swap. Participants could select as many of the available
product swaps as they desired.
Regardless of the specific treatments, our results show that the effect of offering product
swap recommendations was strong (n = 1070) - 88% of participants swapped at least one
product and had a mean basket GHG reduction of 25% (SD = 18%). Participants exposed to
T(Targeted) were 1.5 more likely to choose the most effective GHG-reducing swap. Overall,

neither T(Targeted) nor T(Info) resulted in a significant reduction in basket GHG emissions.
However, T(Info) did have a strong effect on many outcome variables for daily meat-eating
(DME) participants: compared against DMEs in C, DMEs in T(Info) reduced their GHG
by 6 percentage points more (p < 0.05) (an increase of 44%) and had a 12 percentage point
higher willingness-to-swap meat (p < 0.01) (an increase of 52%). T(Info) also resulted in
increased self-efficacy amongst DMEs to reduce their animal product consumption by half.
Policymakers looking to shift dietary behaviour towards more plant consumption can
benefit from our research as it highlights how pre-checkout, basket-level product swap rec-
ommendations can be an effective method to encourage purchases of plant-based foods. Our
research also highlights how recommending product swaps with their GHG reduction in-
formation is particularly effective for frequent meat eaters, the most important consumer
group to address in this regard. Our results should be viewed in light of certain limitations,
namely the external validity of the online supermarket experiment environment and the use
of a representative basket. Future research should focus on implementing and examining
these pre-checkout, basket-level swap recommendations in field studies.
References
[1] W. Willett, J. Rockström, B. Loken, M. Springmann, T. Lang, S. Vermeulen, T. Gar-
nett, D. Tilman, F. DeClerck, A. Wood, M. Jonell, M. Clark, L. J. Gordon, J. Fanzo,
C. Hawkes, R. Zurayk, J. A. Rivera, W. D. Vries, L. M. Sibanda, A. Afshin, A. Chaud-
hary, M. Herrero, R. Agustina, F. Branca, A. Lartey, S. Fan, B. Crona, E. Fox, V. Bignet,
M. Troell, T. Lindahl, S. Singh, S. E. Cornell, K. S. Reddy, S. Narain, S. Nishtar,
C. J. L. Murray, Food in the Anthropocene: the EAT–Lancet Commission on healthy
diets from sustainable food systems, The Lancet 393 (2019) 447–492. doi:10.1016/s0140-
6736(18)31788-4.
[2] P. R. Shukla, J. Skeg, E. C. Buendia, V. Masson-Delmotte, H.-O. Pörtner, D. Roberts,
P. Zhai, R. Slade, S. Connors, S. V. Diemen, et al., Climate Change and Land: an
IPCC special report on climate change, desertification, land degradation, sustainable
land management, food security, and greenhouse gas fluxes in terrestrial ecosystems,
Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) (2019).
[3] K. S. Stylianou, V. L. Fulgoni, O. Jolliet,
Small targeted dietary changes can yield
substantial gains for human health and the environment, Nature Food 2 (2021) 616–627.
doi:10.1038/s43016-021-00343-4.
[4] J. Poore, T. Nemecek, Reducing food’s environmental impacts through producers and
consumers, Science 360 (2018) 987–992. doi:10.1126/science.aaq0216.
[5] J. D. Boer, H. Schösler, J. J. Boersema, Climate change and meat eating: An inconvenient
couple?, Journal of Environmental Psychology 33 (2013) 1–8.
[6] G. Cairns, A critical review of evidence on the sociocultural impacts of food marketing
and policy implications, Appetite 136 (2019) 193–207.

[7] I. Vermeir, B. Weijters, J. D. Houwer, M. Geuens, H. Slabbinck, A. Spruyt, A. V. Ker-
ckhove, W. V. Lippevelde, H. D. Steur, W. Verbeke, Environmentally Sustainable Food
Consumption: A Review and Research Agenda From a Goal-Directed Perspective, Fron-
tiers in Psychology 11 (2020) 1–24. doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2020.01603.
[8] A. H. Grummon, C. J. Y. Lee, T. N. Robinson, E. B. Rimm, D. Rose, Simple dietary
substitutions can reduce carbon footprints and improve dietary quality across diverse
segments of the US population, Nature Food (2023) 1–12. doi:10.1038/s43016-023-00864-
0.
